findings.message: The ad directly attributes body and energy states to the viewer, including 'your midsection,' 'you feel drained,' and 'your drive isn't what it used to be.' That is a personal-attribute style claim about the viewer's body/health.
fixGuidance: Rewrite personal-attribute claims into non-personal educational framing. The word "testosterone" is allowed by itself; avoid phrasing that claims knowledge of the viewer's testosterone or body state.

observations: “your midsection”
“Why you feel drained by 3 p.m.”
“Why workouts feel flat. Why your drive isn't what it used to be.”
policyTrace: Meta Privacy Violations and Personal Attributes: ads may not imply knowledge of the viewer's medical, health, or body status.
The copy repeatedly speaks as if it knows the viewer's own body condition and energy level.

revisionGuidance: Recast the ad as general wellness/product education instead of a body-shame or hidden-cause narrative.
Remove direct viewer-specific body/energy claims and any age or diagnosis implications.
Keep 'testosterone' only as general category/product language if used; do not tie it to a viewer-specific condition or implied diagnosis.
Avoid before/after creative and replace it with neutral product or lifestyle imagery.
If you keep customer stats or scientific language, add clear substantiation and context so the destination page fully supports the claim.

findings.title: Hidden-cause / sensational framing
findings.message: The copy uses hidden-cause and pseudo-scientific framing to explain body and energy changes, then pushes the product as the solution. Phrases like 'what's shifting inside' and 'research shows starts around 30' are presented as authoritative cause-and-effect without sufficient substantiation.
fixGuidance: Remove hidden-cause or deceptive urgency framing such as "secretly crashing" and rewrite the claim as a neutral, substantiated article hook.

findings.title: Before/after transformation creative
findings.message: The image uses a clear transformation comparison: a slumped, tired figure on the left and a smiling, improved figure on the right, with the headline 'FROM DRAINED TO “FEELING LIKE MYSELF” AGAIN.' That is classic before/after body-result framing and reinforces the same personal-attribute pressure as the copy.
fixGuidance: Replace or revise visuals that imply misleading medical authority, fake scientific validation, hidden harm, or direct personal-attribute targeting.
